terms.grammar: verb, third conjugation, transitive; of animals, people, fruit
evidence: Cato Agr. 64.1: oleam (cōgere), to gather (Lewis & Short)
Traupman 107: round up, cōgō, cōgere, coēgī, coāctum
terms.comment: From co-agō, “drive together”: the shepherd’s verb for bringing in the flock.

terms.gloss: pick up, gather one by one (shells, acorns, leaves)
evidence: Cic. de Or. 2.22: conchās eōs et umbilīcōs ad Cajētam et ad Laurentum legere cōnsuēsse
terms.comment: The verb for picking things up off the ground one at a time; see also “pick”.

phrases.english: Let’s gather the dolls and balls.
Let’s collect shells on the beach.
Let’s collect red and yellow leaves.

phrases.latin: conchās eōs et umbilīcōs ad Cajētam et ad Laurentum legere cōnsuēsse et ad omnem animī remissiōnem lūdumque dēscendere
phrases.english: that they used to collect shells and pebbles at Caieta and Laurentum, and stoop to every kind of relaxation and play (Scipio and Laelius, on holiday)

phrases.latin: repente ut conchās legerent galeāsque et sinūs replērent imperāvit
phrases.english: suddenly he ordered them to collect shells and fill their helmets and the folds of their clothes

sources: Lewis & Short: colligo · Lewis & Short: lego · Lewis & Short: concha
Lewis & Short: cogo
John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, pp. 33, 107, 320.
